clue.text: Barberous French news purveyor was noted

definitions.text: Barberous French news purveyor was noted

parts.words: Barberous French news purveyor was noted
parts.note: one name covers Le ..., the Paris daily paper, and the barber of Seville whom Rossini and Mozart set to music, so he was 'noted' in the musical sense

explanation.surface: A barbarous French newspaper man once became famous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barberous' is a play on 'barbarous', pointing to the barber of Rossini's opera; 'noted' means set to musical notes. The clue runs on into 5-across with its trailing dots.
explanation.definitionFit: The Paris newspaper and the operatic barber of Seville share the one name, and the barber was famously put into opera.

clue.text: Ben Jonson loved Shakespeare on this side of it

definitions.text: Ben Jonson loved Shakespeare on this side of it

parts.words: Ben Jonson loved Shakespeare on this side of it
parts.note: a quotation from Jonson's Timber: 'I loved the man, and do honour his memory, on this side' of excessive worship, which supplies the missing word

explanation.surface: A literary fact about Jonson's fondness for his rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson wrote of Shakespeare that he 'loved the man ... on this side idolatry', meaning just short of worshipping him.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonson's famous phrase stops his admiration just short of worship of an idol, the word that completes the quotation.

clue.text: What, by order, a Spanish captain's daughter never did

definitions.text: What, by order, a Spanish captain's daughter never did

parts.words: What, by order, a Spanish captain's daughter never did
parts.note: the folk song No, John, No has a girl whose father, a Spanish captain, bid her always answer no, so on his order she never agreed

explanation.surface: A riddle about an obedient girl and her seafaring father.
explanation.walkthrough: In the song 'No, John, No', the singer says 'My father was a Spanish captain ... bid me always answer no', so she never said yes. 'By order' looks like an anagram signal but means at her father's command.
explanation.definitionFit: The daughter was told always to refuse, so she never agreed or said yes to anything.

clue.text: Has a patient a choice about the time for having it?

definitions.text: Has a patient a choice about the time for having it?

parts.words: Has a patient a choice about the time for having it?
parts.note: the clue asks whether someone in hospital can pick when surgery happens, describing the surgical procedure itself

explanation.surface: A question about hospital scheduling and patient choice.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgical procedure is what a patient undergoes, often at a time set by the surgeon rather than chosen.

clue.text: … for everything he did

parts.note: continuing from 1-across, the barber of the opera sings that he is the man who does everything for the town, from the Latin phrase 'do everything'

explanation.surface: The barber was famous for doing it all.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots join this clue to 1-across: Figaro's aria 'Largo al factotum' calls him the town's do-everything, from Latin fac totum, 'do all'.
explanation.definitionFit: A general handyman or servant does all kinds of jobs; the Latin roots mean 'do all'.

clue.text: Along which time flies, relatively speaking

definitions.text: Along which time flies, relatively speaking

parts.words: Along which time flies, relatively speaking
parts.note: in Einstein's relativity, time is treated as an extra axis beyond length, width and height, along which events move

explanation.surface: A playful remark on how fast time passes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relatively speaking' looks like a casual aside but points to Einstein's theory of relativity, where time is added to the three spatial axes.
explanation.definitionFit: In relativity, time is the extra axis added to the three of space.

clue.text: In column form it's prohibited by deity

parts.note: tabu is a spelling of taboo, forbidden
a lar is a Roman household god

explanation.surface: Something laid out in columns is forbidden by a god.
explanation.walkthrough: LAR is one of the Lares, Roman household gods; 'by' just joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Data set out in rows and columns forms a table.

clue.text: Like jackdaw, like magpie

definitions.meaning: jackdaws are known for stealing shiny things
magpies are also proverbial pilferers of bright objects

explanation.surface: A comparison of two birds of the crow family.
explanation.definitionFit: Both birds have a reputation for stealing, so each is given to theft.

clue.text: Pitcairn settler with no wish to return to "Blighty "?

definitions.text: Pitcairn settler with no wish to return to "Blighty "?

parts.words: Pitcairn settler with no wish to return to "Blighty "?
parts.note: the Pitcairn Islanders descend from the Bounty rebels, who did not want to go back to Captain Bligh, and 'Blighty' is also slang for Britain

explanation.surface: A Pitcairn islander with no homesickness for Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blighty' is soldiers' slang for Britain, but here it also means Captain Bligh's ship: the Bounty rebels settled Pitcairn rather than face him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bounty's rebel sailors, who rose against Captain Bligh, founded the Pitcairn settlement.

clue.text: Robinson loses his head but sounds so philosophical.

definitions.note: the clue's adjective stands for the noun, a philosopher of the Enlightenment

indicators.note: losing his head means the castaway's surname drops its first letter
the word sounds tells us the beheaded name is said out loud to give a similar-sounding name

parts.note: Robinson Crusoe, Defoe's castaway, gives his surname

explanation.surface: Robinson is beheaded yet still talks like a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: Robinson is Defoe's castaway Robinson Crusoe. Said aloud, his surname is the philosopher's name with a C in front; 'loses his head' drops that C. 'But' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Jacques, the Genevan thinker behind The Social Contract, is a philosopher.

clue.text: The boot is put into the player

indicators.note: the letters of the words are put into a new shape, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A footballer's boot is aimed at another player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put into' looks like a container but rearranges BOOTIS.
explanation.definitionFit: An oboe player is a musician, a player in an orchestra.

clue.text: Being idle makes Annie fat

indicators.note: makes means the letters are made into something new, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Lazing about makes Annie put on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes' signals that ANNIEFAT is turned into a new word; 'Being' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A French borrowing for a do-nothing, meaning lazy or work-shy.

clue.text: But it's non-plussed in test cricket

definitions.text: But it's non-plussed in test cricket

parts.words: But it's non-plussed in test cricket
parts.note: a cricket team names twelve, but the twelfth man does not play, so the side without the one extra is the number of players

explanation.surface: A remark that something is unflustered in a Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricket side is the players on the field; the twelfth man is a substitute, so take away the plus one and the team is one fewer. 'Non-plussed' looks like 'bewildered'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket team fielded in a Test has this number of players, and is itself called by that number.

clue.text: Bad man always takes in the Italian party

indicators.note: takes in means the word for always holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: always means for ever
il is Italian for the
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A villain who keeps gatecrashing Italian parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Italian' is a translation device: the solver must give the Italian article. 'Bad man' sits at the front, not 'party'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrongdoer or villain is a bad man.

clue.text: Get around in French direction-finder

parts.note: en is French for in
a compass finds north and so direction

explanation.surface: Getting about in France with a compass.
explanation.definitionFit: To surround or enclose something is to get around it.

clue.text: Polar flier as one might expect

definitions.text: Polar flier as one might expect

parts.words: Polar flier as one might expect
parts.note: the American aviator who flew over the poles had a name that sounds just like a winged creature, fitting for a flier

explanation.surface: An Arctic bird, just as you'd expect.
explanation.walkthrough: Admiral Richard Byrd was the American explorer who flew over the South Pole; his name sounds like 'bird', what one would expect a flier to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Admiral Richard Byrd made pioneering flights over the poles, and his surname suits any winged flier.

clue.text: Diurnal do-gooder

parts.note: a member of the Scout movement promises to do a good turn every day

explanation.surface: Someone who does good by day.
explanation.walkthrough: Scouts pledge a good turn daily, so 'diurnal' (daily) marks the do-gooder.
explanation.definitionFit: Scouts famously do a good turn each day.

clue.text: A check on the presents ?

parts.note: 'the presents' reads as gifts but means the people present, whose attendance is checked by calling names

explanation.surface: An inventory of gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presents' tempts one to think of gifts; here it means those who are present.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling out names to see who is there checks attendance.

clue.text: Fish lady, so obliging

definitions.meaning: a fish of the trout family
a charlady or cleaning woman, who traditionally 'obliges' by doing housework

explanation.surface: A fishwife who is very helpful.
explanation.walkthrough: A char (charwoman) is a daily cleaner; such a woman was said to 'oblige' her employer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a trout-like fish and also a cleaning woman who obliges with the housework.

clue.text: One summoned by a fiery cross

definitions.text: One summoned by a fiery cross

parts.words: One summoned by a fiery cross
parts.note: in the Scottish Highlands a burning cross was carried round to call members of a clan to arms

explanation.surface: Someone called out by a burning cross.
explanation.walkthrough: The fiery cross was the Highland signal to gather a clan for war.
explanation.definitionFit: A clan member was called to arms by the burning cross carried through Highland glens.

clue.text: Disc jockey with a French following acts without extras

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the word acts goes round the other pieces

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: following says the French article comes after the disc jockey abbreviation

parts.note: un is French for a

explanation.surface: A DJ with a French fan base performs with no backing singers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but is the old sense 'outside', so the performers' word wraps the rest; the definition hides in the surface's 'no extras'.
explanation.definitionFit: Additions or accessories are supplementary extras.

clue.text: It's hostile in one archangel to drop high explosive

parts.note: taken as written
one is I as a Roman numeral

indicators.note: to drop means the explosive's letters are let fall out of the angel's name

parts.note: Michael is one of the archangels

explanation.surface: Something hostile among the angels drops a bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: MICHAEL without HE leaves MICAL; 'It's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfriendly or opposed, as an enemy is.

clue.text: Unwelcome 18's to injuries

parts.note: 18 is extras, so these are unwelcome extras to injuries, as in the saying about adding offensive remarks to injury

explanation.surface: Unwanted additions to someone's wounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 18-down is ADJUNCTS (extras); the idiom 'adding insult to injury' supplies the unwelcome extras.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb speaks of adding offensive words or slights to injury, the unwelcome additions.

clue.text: Going it, i.e., playing ducks and drakes with money?

definitions.text: Going it, i.e., playing ducks and drakes with money?

parts.words: Going it, i.e., playing ducks and drakes with money?
parts.note: spending lavishly, squandering money, is to have a go at it; ducks and drakes is skimming stones across water, which throws up spray

explanation.surface: Squandering cash like a child skimming stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing ducks and drakes with money' is an idiom for wasting it; to splash out is to spend freely, and a skimmed stone splashes.
explanation.definitionFit: To spend lavishly is to splash out, and a stone skipped across water lands with a splash.

clue.text: Numbers in love go to America, it's divine

parts.note: Num is the abbreviation for the Old Testament book Numbers
taken as written
love is zero in tennis, the letter O
US is America

explanation.surface: Numbers in love emigrate to America, which seems heavenly.
explanation.walkthrough: Numbers is a book of the Bible, abbreviated NUM; 'go to' and 'it's' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something holy or godlike has a sense of the sacred about it.

clue.text: …and divinely ambiguous may its answer be

definitions.text: …and divinely ambiguous may its answer be

parts.words: …and divinely ambiguous may its answer be
parts.note: the Greek shrine at Delphi gave inspired replies that famously could be read two ways

explanation.surface: Continuing from 21: the divine reply may be unclear.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots join this to 21-across's 'divine'; the oracle at Delphi was famous for answers with double meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A prophet or shrine gives inspired answers, often riddling, like Delphi's.

clue.text: Seeing as a chum's in a bit of trouble

indicators.note: being in trouble means the letters are in disorder, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Since a friend is in a spot of bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a bit of trouble' signals that ACHUMSIN is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Means 'since' or 'because', introducing a reason.

clue.text: Scottish charm

parts.note: 'Scottish' points to Sir Walter Scott, whose novel of the Crusades bears the title of a lucky amulet

explanation.surface: The charm of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scottish' means by Sir Walter Scott, the Scottish novelist who wrote The Talisman (1825).
explanation.definitionFit: A lucky charm or amulet, and the title of a novel by Sir Walter Scott.

clue.text: Cosy home in the Union ? Most rational

parts.note: the Union of South Africa, abbreviated SA
a nest is a cosy home

explanation.surface: A snug home in the Union is the most sensible choice.
explanation.walkthrough: The Union of South Africa (1910-61) was the country's formal name, so 'the Union' gave SA in older puzzles; 'in' is a link, not a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of sane, the most sensible.
